figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic of a Symmetric Li-LLZO Cell with Li Metal as Both the Working and Counter Electrode The cell is cycling within a mechanical testing unit that controls the applied stack pressure.

Figure 2. The Potential Response to a Constant Current Density at Varying Stack Pressures The potential is normalized to the initial potential at the beginning of the constant current cycling. The potential responses for four different current densities are shown.

Figure 3. The Electrochemical Behavior under Varying Stack Pressure (A) The potential response under a constant current of 0.1 mA cm2 while increasing and decreasing the stack pressure above the ‘‘critical stack pressure.’’ Artifacts of the AC signal superimposed onto the DC signal are noticeable at the end of each pressure step. (B) Representative EIS spectra at high (2.4 MPa) and low (1.2 MPa) stack pressure: inset highlights low frequency electrochemical reaction (ECR) behavior. (C) The Rint calculated from the EIS taken at the end of each pressure step for each cycle.

Figure 4. The Incorporation of a Reference Electrode for Decoupling Stripping and Plating Behavior (A) Schematic of the three-electrode setup with a Ni reference electrode. (B) Top view illustrating the geometry of the LLZO billet with a third face cut perpendicular to the billet face. (C) EIS between the three different electrodes, showing blocking behavior for the Li-Ni conﬁgurations and non-blocking behavior for the Li-Li conﬁgurations.

Figure 5. Potential Response under a Constant Current Density of 0.2 mA cm2 and Decreasing Stack Pressures The usage of the Ni reference electrode allows for the decoupling of the Li stripping electrode (WE) and the Li plating electrode (CE).

Figure 6. The Potential Response to Both Li Stripping and Plating at a Constant Current Density of 0.2 mA cm2 at a Representative High Stack Pressure and Representative Low Stack Pressure 0.35 mA cm2 of Li is stripped and plated each cycle.

Figure 7. The Proposed Depletion of Li at the Li-Electrolyte Interface during Cycling (A) The proposed microstructure of the Li-electrolyte interface above the ‘‘critical stack pressure’’ where the magnitude of the applied pressure is sufﬁcient to maintain contact between Li and electrolyte. (B) The proposed microstructure of the interface below the ‘‘critical stack pressure’’ where the applied pressure is insufﬁcient to replenish the Li at the interface, resulting in void formation at the interface and a subsequent reduction in the contact area.

Figure 8. Comparison of the Pressure-Induced Strain Rate and the Current-Induced Strain Rate for Cycling at 0.1 mA cm2 The point at which the current-induced strain rate exceeds the pressure-induced strain rate is likely the point at which unstable void growth occurs, as evidenced by a decrease in the contact area, resulting in dramatic polarization.

The same polarization behavior is observed for both compositions at the same stack pressures.
